items.passage: The floor of the deep ocean holds potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules, rich in nickel, cobalt and manganese. These metals are essential for electric vehicle batteries, and demand for them is expected to grow sharply as countries move away from petrol cars. Mining companies argue that harvesting nodules from the seabed is less destructive than opening new mines on land, which often displace communities and clear forests. Critics reply that the deep ocean is one of the least studied places on Earth, and that scraping the seabed could destroy habitats that took millions of years to form. The International Seabed Authority, which regulates mining in international waters, has been working for years on a set of rules, but member states remain divided. Some Pacific island nations support mining because the royalties could fund schools and hospitals. Others, including several European countries, want a pause until scientists understand the risks better. Meanwhile, the companies waiting for licences say delay itself has a cost: every year without seabed metals is another year of reliance on land mines with their own environmental damage. items.passage: Public libraries are often described as quiet rooms full of books, but their real value is harder to measure. In many towns, the library is the only place where a person can use a computer, print a form, or sit for hours without being asked to buy something. Librarians now help visitors apply for jobs, learn to use government websites, and find reliable health information. This work is rarely counted in the statistics that councils use when they decide budgets. When a library closes, the loss shows up slowly: students lose a study space, older residents lose a meeting place, and job seekers lose free internet access. Supporters of libraries argue that funding them is cheaper than dealing with the problems that follow their closure, such as lower literacy and greater isolation. Critics reply that in an age when almost everything is available on a phone, maintaining large buildings full of books is an expensive habit. The evidence, however, points the other way. Towns that kept their libraries open during the last decade report higher rates of adult learning and stronger community groups. A library, the passage suggests, is less a warehouse for books than a piece of public infrastructure, as basic as a road or a water supply, and it should be judged the way infrastructure is judged: by what a town cannot do without it.

items.passage: On a hot summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside a few kilometres away. This difference, called the urban heat island effect, is caused by the materials cities are built from. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, while the lack of trees means there is little shade and little cooling from evaporation. Traffic and air conditioners add more heat to streets that are already warm. The effect is not evenly shared. Poorer neighbourhoods, which often have fewer parks and more paved surfaces, tend to be hotter than wealthier areas with gardens and tree-lined streets. During heatwaves, this gap can become a matter of health: older people and those with heart conditions suffer most when nights stay warm and the body cannot cool down. Cities have begun to respond. Some paint roofs white to reflect sunlight, others plant trees along streets, and a few are replacing asphalt with porous materials that let rainwater through. These measures work best when they are aimed at the hottest neighbourhoods first. The lesson of the heat island is that a city's temperature is not only a matter of weather. It is also a result of the choices made about what a city is built from and for whom it is built.
